opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the honest starting point is that jailbreak defenses today are much weaker than people often assume. Almost every frontier model we've red-teamed at FAR.AI can be jailbroken with enough effort, and often not that much effort. For a long time that was tolerable, because the worst a jailbroken model could do was write something offensive or give you information you could find with a search engine. As capabilities grow, that calculus changes. If a model can meaningfully uplift someone trying to synthesize a pathogen or carry out a sophisticated cyberattack, then a 95% effective defense isn't good enough, because attackers only need to find the 5%.

So a few things need to change.

First, we need to stop treating robustness as something that comes for free with scale. There was hope that bigger, smarter models would naturally become harder to trick, since they'd better understand what the user is really asking for. Our research suggests it isn't that simple. Some of our work on superhuman Go AIs found that systems far stronger than any human player could still be beaten by fairly simple adversarial strategies. Capability and robustness are different properties, and you have to invest in robustness directly.

Second, defenses need to be layered. Relying only on the model's refusal training is fragile. You want input and output classifiers, monitoring of usage patterns over time, and controls on who gets access to the most dangerous capabilities. Each layer has holes, but stacking them makes attacks much more expensive. Anthropic's constitutional classifiers work is a good example of how much you can gain from a dedicated defensive layer, even if it isn't perfect.

Third, we have to think about threat models beyond the chat box. Many models now offer fine-tuning APIs, and we've shown that fine-tuning on even a small amount of harmful data can strip out safety training almost entirely. Open-weight models are harder still, because once the weights are out, any safeguard can be removed. As capabilities rise, developers and policymakers need to be much more deliberate about which capabilities get released in which form.

Finally, there's a measurement problem. A lot of safety evaluations are run by the developers themselves against static benchmarks, and attackers adapt. We need more adaptive, adversarial evaluation from independent third parties, more like how security is tested in other critical industries. If you can't measure how robust your system is against a motivated adversary, you're mostly guessing.

The core point is that the bar has to rise in step with capabilities. Defenses that are fine for a chatbot won't be fine for a system that can act autonomously in the world or provide real expert-level uplift. That gap is closing faster than our defenses are improving, and I think that's one of the most important problems in AI safety right now.

r001.rationale: The response says almost every frontier model the team has red-teamed can be jailbroken with enough effort, not that a universal jailbreak exists for every current model.

r002.rationale: It says attackers need to find only a small gap in a defense, but does not predict that they will invest more effort as models become more capable.

r003.rationale: The response does not identify improving defenses on the least robust models as the lowest-hanging fruit.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. So the short version is that I think the field has been grading itself on a curve, and that's going to stop working.

Right now most jailbreak defenses are evaluated against a fairly fixed set of attacks: known prompt-injection patterns, role-play framings, a few optimized adversarial suffixes. And on those benchmarks things look okay. But the thing we keep finding at FAR.AI is that when you give a competent red team a few days and a modest budget, basically every deployed system falls over. The gap between "robust against the attacks we tested" and "robust against an adversary who's actually trying" is enormous, and it's been enormous for years.

As models get more capable, that gap gets more expensive in two ways. First, the harm ceiling rises. A jailbroken model that can write a phishing email is annoying. A jailbroken model that can walk someone through a serious bio or cyber uplift is a different category of problem, and you can't just accept a 5% attack success rate on that. Second, and this is underappreciated, the attackers get the capable models too. A lot of the most effective jailbreaks we've seen recently were generated or refined by other models. So you're in an arms race where both sides are scaling, and right now the offense scales better.

So what needs to change? A few things.

One, we need to stop treating this as a classifier problem and start treating it as a security problem. That means adversarial evaluation as a first-class requirement, with the budget and expertise that implies, not a checkbox at the end of training. It means thinking about defense in depth rather than one model refusing well. Input filters, output filters, monitoring on the deployment side, rate limiting on suspicious usage. None of those are individually robust, but stacking them changes the economics for the attacker.

Two, I think we should be much more honest about what the base model's safety training can actually bear. Fine-tuning for refusal is shallow. We've shown you can undo it with a handful of examples, and a lot of jailbreaks work precisely because they're finding the shallow boundary. For the highest-stakes capabilities, I'd rather see them not be in the deployed model at all, through data filtering or unlearning, than rely on a refusal layer that we know is brittle.

Three, we need better science on what robustness even means here. In vision we had a decade of adversarial examples work, and the lesson was humbling: almost every defense that wasn't adversarial training in some form got broken within months. I expect the same here. So I'd put a lot more weight on defenses that come with some kind of guarantee or at least a clear threat model, and much less on "we tried some attacks and it held up."

And the last point is about governance more than technique. If a lab can't demonstrate robustness against a well-resourced red team, that should actually constrain what capabilities they deploy and to whom. Right now the incentive is to ship and patch. For most capabilities that's fine. For the dangerous tail, I don't think it is, and I'd like to see that become a norm, or a requirement, before we learn the lesson the hard way.

r001.rationale: The response says competent red teams can break deployed systems, but does not state that a universal jailbreak can be found for every current model.

r002.rationale: It says attackers can use capable models and that offense scales better, but does not predict they will invest more effort as models become more capable.

r003.rationale: The response recommends stronger adversarial evaluation and layered defenses, but does not identify improving the least robust models as the lowest-hanging fruit.

astra-6.text:
I think we need to move from defenses that stop the attacks we already know about to defenses that hold up against someone actively trying to break them. Those are very different standards. You can train a model on a collection of jailbreaks and get impressive results, but an attacker gets to adapt to whatever defense you deploy.

As models become more capable, the consequences of a failure can also grow. If a model is just producing text, that’s one threat model. If it can execute code, access sensitive information, or take actions on your behalf, then a jailbreak could cross a much more consequential boundary. So we need to evaluate the whole system, including what tools it can use and what permissions it has.

I’d want both stronger adversarial training and defense in depth. Make the model more robust, but also limit its permissions and enforce critical restrictions outside the model. We shouldn’t depend on a model always following an instruction to keep a secret if we can avoid giving it access to that secret in the first place.

And we need to be honest about what our evaluations establish. Failing to find a jailbreak isn’t the same as showing that one doesn’t exist. The important question is how much sustained, adaptive effort a defense has survived, and whether that level of assurance is appropriate for the capabilities we’re deploying.

r001.rationale: The response says attackers can adapt and that a defense surviving effort matters, but it does not claim that every current model can be jailbroken with enough effort.

r002.rationale: It discusses adaptive attackers and greater consequences as models gain capabilities, but does not predict that attackers will invest more effort in jailbreaking them.

r003.rationale: It recommends stronger defenses and defense in depth, but does not identify improving the least robust models as the current lowest-hanging fruit.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the big shift we need is from defenses that work against the attacks we happen to know about to defenses that hold up against an adversary who is actively trying to break them. Those are quite different standards. You can train a model on a collection of jailbreaks and get very good results on that collection, but that doesn't necessarily tell you how it will behave when someone develops a new attack specifically against your defense.

As models become more capable, we should also expect attackers to use those capabilities. They can automate the search for jailbreaks, adapt to feedback, and explore far more possibilities than a human could manually. So evaluations need to give attackers a meaningful opportunity to adapt, rather than just testing a fixed list of prompts.

And then I think we need defense in depth. If a model is using tools or accessing sensitive information, we shouldn't make the security of the whole system depend on whether it follows an instruction in its context. We should have permissions, isolation, and checks on consequential actions. Improving the model's robustness is important, but so is limiting what a successful jailbreak can actually do.

r001.rationale: The response discusses adapting attacks and testing defenses, but does not say that enough effort can find a universal jailbreak for every current model.

r002.rationale: It predicts attackers will use models’ capabilities to automate and adapt attacks, but does not state they will be willing to invest more effort as models become more capable.

r003.rationale: It recommends stronger evaluations and defense in depth, but does not identify the least robust models’ defenses as the current lowest-hanging fruit.
